Domain and range

Fractions

p(x)q(x):  q(x)≠0\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}:\ \ q(x) \ne 0q(x)p(x)​:  q(x)=0

The idea

You cannot divide by zero, so remove every xxx that makes the denominator vanish. Solve q(x)=0q(x) = 0q(x)=0 and exclude those values; on the graph they are vertical asymptotes (or holes).

Worked example

f(x)=x+1x2−4f(x) = \tfrac{x + 1}{x^2 - 4}f(x)=x2−4x+1​: x2−4=0x^2 - 4 = 0x2−4=0 at x=±2x = \pm 2x=±2, so the domain is R∖{−2,2}\mathbb R \setminus \{-2, 2\}R∖{−2,2}.

Even roots

g(x)2k:  g(x)≥0\sqrt[2k]{g(x)}:\ \ g(x) \ge 02kg(x)​:  g(x)≥0

The idea

A square root (or 4th, 6th… root) of a negative number is not real, so the inside must be ≥0\ge 0≥0. Solve that inequality; the graph starts at the point where the inside is zero. Odd roots ( 3\sqrt[3]{\ }3 ​) accept every real number.

Worked example

f(x)=6−2xf(x) = \sqrt{6 - 2x}f(x)=6−2x​: 6−2x≥0  ⟺  x≤36 - 2x \ge 0 \iff x \le 36−2x≥0⟺x≤3, so D=(−∞,3]D = (-\infty, 3]D=(−∞,3]. The graph ends at (3,0)(3, 0)(3,0).

Logarithms

log⁡ag(x):  g(x)>0\log_a g(x):\ \ g(x) > 0loga​g(x):  g(x)>0

The idea

A logarithm only accepts positive numbers — strictly: log⁡0\log 0log0 is undefined too. So require the inside >0> 0>0; at the boundary the graph has a vertical asymptote going down to −∞-\infty−∞.

Worked example

f(x)=ln⁡(x−3)f(x) = \ln(x - 3)f(x)=ln(x−3): x−3>0  ⟺  x>3x - 3 > 0 \iff x > 3x−3>0⟺x>3. For ln⁡(9−x2)\ln(9 - x^2)ln(9−x2) you need x2<9x^2 < 9x2<9, i.e. −3<x<3-3 < x < 3−3<x<3.

tan and the inverse functions

tan⁡x: x≠π2+kπ\tan x:\ x \ne \tfrac\pi2 + k\pitanx: x=2π​+kπarcsin⁡x,arccos⁡x:  ∣x∣≤1\arcsin x, \arccos x:\ \ |x| \le 1arcsinx,arccosx:  ∣x∣≤1

The idea

tan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡x\tan x = \tfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}tanx=cosxsinx​ is a fraction, undefined where cos⁡x=0\cos x = 0cosx=0. arcsin⁡\arcsinarcsin and arccos⁡\arccosarccos undo sin⁡\sinsin and cos⁡\coscos, whose values lie in [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1] — so only those numbers can go in.

Ranges to remember

ex>0e^x > 0ex>0x2≥0x^2 \ge 0x2≥0−1≤sin⁡x,cos⁡x≤1-1 \le \sin x, \cos x \le 1−1≤sinx,cosx≤1x+1x≥2 (x>0)x + \tfrac1x \ge 2 \ (x > 0)x+x1​≥2 (x>0)

The idea

Many ranges come from a few facts: exe^xex is always positive, squares are never negative, sin⁡\sinsin and cos⁡\coscos stay between −1-1−1 and 111, and x+1x≥2x + \tfrac1x \ge 2x+x1​≥2 for x>0x > 0x>0 (equality at x=1x = 1x=1). Build the range of a formula from these bounds.

Worked example

f(x)=3+2sin⁡xf(x) = 3 + 2\sin xf(x)=3+2sinx: from −1≤sin⁡x≤1-1 \le \sin x \le 1−1≤sinx≤1, multiply by 2 and add 3: 1≤f(x)≤51 \le f(x) \le 51≤f(x)≤5.

Range by solving for x

y=f(x) ⇒ x=g(y),f(D)=Dom⁡gy = f(x) \ \Rightarrow\ x = g(y), \quad f(D) = \operatorname{Dom} gy=f(x) ⇒ x=g(y),f(D)=Domg

Solve for x and see which values of y are allowed.

Symbols: DDD: the domain of fff; f(D)f(D)f(D): its range (all the values it takes).

The idea

A value yyy is in the range exactly when y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x) has a solution xxx in the domain. So solve for xxx in terms of yyy and see which yyy are allowed — those form the range.

Worked example

y=2x+1x−1y = \tfrac{2x + 1}{x - 1}y=x−12x+1​: y(x−1)=2x+1⇒x(y−2)=y+1⇒x=y+1y−2y(x - 1) = 2x + 1 \Rightarrow x(y - 2) = y + 1 \Rightarrow x = \tfrac{y + 1}{y - 2}y(x−1)=2x+1⇒x(y−2)=y+1⇒x=y−2y+1​. This works unless y=2y = 2y=2, so the range is R∖{2}\mathbb R \setminus \{2\}R∖{2} — the horizontal asymptote.

Composition and inverse

Composition

(f∘g)(x)=f(g(x))(f \circ g)(x) = f\big(g(x)\big)(f∘g)(x)=f(g(x))f∘g≠g∘ff \circ g \ne g \circ ff∘g=g∘f

Symbols: f∘gf \circ gf∘g (“fff after ggg”): apply ggg first, then fff.

The idea

f∘gf \circ gf∘g means “do ggg first, then fff”: put g(x)g(x)g(x) in place of every xxx in fff. The order matters — squaring then adding 1 is not the same as adding 1 then squaring.

Worked example

f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2, g(x)=x+1g(x) = x + 1g(x)=x+1: (f∘g)(x)=(x+1)2(f \circ g)(x) = (x + 1)^2(f∘g)(x)=(x+1)2 (yellow) but (g∘f)(x)=x2+1(g \circ f)(x) = x^2 + 1(g∘f)(x)=x2+1 (blue). They agree only at x=0x = 0x=0.

Inverse function

y=f(x)  ⟺  x=f−1(y)y = f(x) \iff x = f^{-1}(y)y=f(x)⟺x=f−1(y)f(f−1(x))=xf\big(f^{-1}(x)\big) = xf(f−1(x))=x

Swap x and y and solve for y. It exists when f is one-to-one (strictly monotonic).

The idea

The inverse undoes fff: if fff sends xxx to yyy, then f−1f^{-1}f−1 sends yyy back to xxx. To find it, write y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x), solve for xxx, then rename yyy as xxx. It exists only if fff never takes the same value twice (one-to-one).

Worked example

f(x)=3x−2f(x) = 3x - 2f(x)=3x−2: y=3x−2⇒x=y+23y = 3x - 2 \Rightarrow x = \tfrac{y + 2}{3}y=3x−2⇒x=3y+2​, so f−1(x)=x+23f^{-1}(x) = \tfrac{x + 2}{3}f−1(x)=3x+2​. Check: f(f−1(x))=3⋅x+23−2=xf\big(f^{-1}(x)\big) = 3\cdot\tfrac{x + 2}{3} - 2 = xf(f−1(x))=3⋅3x+2​−2=x.

Graph of the inverse

(a,b)∈f  ⟺  (b,a)∈f−1(a, b) \in f \iff (b, a) \in f^{-1}(a,b)∈f⟺(b,a)∈f−1

Mirror image in the line y=xy = xy=x.

The idea

Swapping xxx and yyy reflects every point in the line y=xy = xy=x. So the graph of f−1f^{-1}f−1 is the mirror image of the graph of fff: exe^xex and ln⁡x\ln xlnx are the classic pair, with (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1) going to (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0).

Worked example

f(x)=x3f(x) = x^3f(x)=x3 passes through (2,8)(2, 8)(2,8), so f−1(x)=x3f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}f−1(x)=3x​ passes through (8,2)(8, 2)(8,2): f−1(8)=2f^{-1}(8) = 2f−1(8)=2.

Domain swaps with range

Dom⁡f−1=f(D)\operatorname{Dom} f^{-1} = f(D)Domf−1=f(D)f−1(f(D))=Df^{-1}(f(D)) = Df−1(f(D))=D

Symbols: Dom⁡\operatorname{Dom}Dom: the domain; f(D)f(D)f(D): the range of fff.

The idea

What goes in to f−1f^{-1}f−1 is what came out of fff. So the domain of f−1f^{-1}f−1 is the range of fff, and the range of f−1f^{-1}f−1 is the domain of fff. Finding the range of fff first tells you where f−1f^{-1}f−1 lives.

Worked example

f(x)=x−1+2f(x) = \sqrt{x - 1} + 2f(x)=x−1​+2 has domain x≥1x \ge 1x≥1 and range y≥2y \ge 2y≥2. Its inverse f−1(x)=(x−2)2+1f^{-1}(x) = (x - 2)^2 + 1f−1(x)=(x−2)2+1 is defined for x≥2x \ge 2x≥2 only (blue curve, right half).

Symmetry, periodicity, monotonicity

Even function

f(−x)=f(x)f(-x) = f(x)f(−x)=f(x)

Symmetric about the yyy-axis: x2x^2x2, cos⁡x\cos xcosx, ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣.

The idea

fff is even if f(−x)=f(x)f(-x) = f(x)f(−x)=f(x): the graph is symmetric about the yyy-axis. Only even powers of xxx, cos⁡x\cos xcosx, ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣… To use it: knowing fff for x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 gives it everywhere.

Worked example

f(x)=x4−3x2f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2f(x)=x4−3x2: f(−x)=(−x)4−3(−x)2=x4−3x2=f(x)f(-x) = (-x)^4 - 3(-x)^2 = x^4 - 3x^2 = f(x)f(−x)=(−x)4−3(−x)2=x4−3x2=f(x), so it is even — the two blue points mirror each other.

Odd function

f(−x)=−f(x)f(-x) = -f(x)f(−x)=−f(x)

Symmetric about the origin: x3x^3x3, sin⁡x\sin xsinx, 1x\tfrac1xx1​. If 000 is in the domain, f(0)=0f(0) = 0f(0)=0.

The idea

fff is odd if f(−x)=−f(x)f(-x) = -f(x)f(−x)=−f(x): turning the graph half a turn about the origin leaves it unchanged. Odd powers, sin⁡x\sin xsinx, tan⁡x\tan xtanx… If an odd fff is defined at 0, then f(0)=0f(0) = 0f(0)=0.

Worked example

f(x)=x3−3xf(x) = x^3 - 3xf(x)=x3−3x: f(−x)=−x3+3x=−f(x)f(-x) = -x^3 + 3x = -f(x)f(−x)=−x3+3x=−f(x), odd. The points (2,2)(2, 2)(2,2) and (−2,−2)(-2, -2)(−2,−2) are symmetric through the origin.

Period

f(x+T)=f(x)f(x + T) = f(x)f(x+T)=f(x)f(ωx):  T∣ω∣f(\omega x):\ \ \frac{T}{|\omega|}f(ωx):  ∣ω∣T​

Symbols: TTT: the period, the smallest shift after which the graph repeats.

The idea

A periodic graph repeats every TTT units. Inside f(ωx)f(\omega x)f(ωx) the variable runs ω\omegaω times faster, so the pattern repeats ∣ω∣\lvert\omega\rvert∣ω∣ times as often: the period is divided by ∣ω∣\lvert\omega\rvert∣ω∣.

Worked example

sin⁡x\sin xsinx has period 2π2\pi2π, so sin⁡(3x)\sin(3x)sin(3x) has period 2π3\tfrac{2\pi}{3}32π​: three full waves where sin⁡x\sin xsinx (dashed) makes one.

Symmetry about a line

f(a+x)=f(a−x)  ⟺  x=af(a + x) = f(a - x) \iff x = af(a+x)=f(a−x)⟺x=a

And f(a+x)+f(a−x)=2bf(a + x) + f(a - x) = 2bf(a+x)+f(a−x)=2b means symmetry about the point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b).

The idea

f(a+x)=f(a−x)f(a + x) = f(a - x)f(a+x)=f(a−x) says: going xxx to the right of aaa or xxx to the left gives the same height. The graph is symmetric about the vertical line x=ax = ax=a — every parabola is, about its axis x=−b2ax = -\tfrac{b}{2a}x=−2ab​.

Worked example

f(x)=x2−6x+1f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 1f(x)=x2−6x+1: −b2a=3-\tfrac{b}{2a} = 3−2ab​=3; check f(3+x)=x2−8=f(3−x)f(3 + x) = x^2 - 8 = f(3 - x)f(3+x)=x2−8=f(3−x). Symmetric about x=3x = 3x=3.

Monotonic

x1<x2⇒f(x1)<f(x2)(↗)x_1 < x_2 \Rightarrow f(x_1) < f(x_2) \quad (\nearrow)x1​<x2​⇒f(x1​)<f(x2​)(↗)

A strictly monotonic function is one-to-one, so equations f(x)=cf(x) = cf(x)=c have at most one solution.

The idea

Increasing means: move right, go up. A function can increase on one interval and decrease on another — the turning points separate them. For differentiable functions, the sign of f′f'f′ decides.

Worked example

f(x)=x2−4xf(x) = x^2 - 4xf(x)=x2−4x has its vertex at x=2x = 2x=2: decreasing on (−∞,2](-\infty, 2](−∞,2], increasing on [2,∞)[2, \infty)[2,∞).

Order of operations

y=a f(b(x−h))+ky = a\,f\big(b(x - h)\big) + ky=af(b(x−h))+k

From fff: squeeze by bbb, shift by hhh, stretch by aaa, shift by kkk.

The idea

For y=a f(b(x−h))+ky = a\,f\big(b(x - h)\big) + ky=af(b(x−h))+k, work from the inside out: squeeze by bbb, shift by hhh horizontally, stretch by aaa vertically, and finally shift by kkk vertically. For a parabola a(x−h)2+ka(x - h)^2 + ka(x−h)2+k the vertex simply goes to (h,k)(h, k)(h,k).

Worked example

y=2(x−1)2+3y = 2(x - 1)^2 + 3y=2(x−1)2+3 from y=x2y = x^2y=x2: right 1, stretch × 2, up 3. Vertex (1,3)(1, 3)(1,3), and the parabola is narrower.

Basic graphs

Linear and quadratic

y=mx+by = mx + by=mx+by=a(x−h)2+ky = a(x - h)^2 + ky=a(x−h)2+k

Parabola opens up when a>0a > 0a>0; vertex (h,k)(h, k)(h,k); axis x=hx = hx=h.

The idea

A line is fixed by its slope mmm (rise over run) and its intercept bbb. A parabola a(x−h)2+ka(x - h)^2 + ka(x−h)2+k has vertex (h,k)(h, k)(h,k); it opens up when a>0a > 0a>0 and down when a<0a < 0a<0.

Worked example

The line through (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) and (3,8)(3, 8)(3,8): m=8−23−1=3m = \tfrac{8 - 2}{3 - 1} = 3m=3−18−2​=3, then 2=3⋅1+b2 = 3\cdot 1 + b2=3⋅1+b gives b=−1b = -1b=−1: y=3x−1y = 3x - 1y=3x−1.

Exponential

y=ax:  (0,1) ✓,y>0y = a^x:\ \ (0, 1)\ \checkmark, \quad y > 0y=ax:  (0,1) ✓,y>0

Increasing when a>1a > 1a>1, decreasing when 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1; asymptote y=0y = 0y=0.

Symbols: aaa: the base (a>0a > 0a>0, a≠1a \ne 1a=1).

The idea

axa^xax (with a>0a > 0a>0) passes through (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1) because a0=1a^0 = 1a0=1, is always positive, and has the xxx-axis as an asymptote on one side. It grows when a>1a > 1a>1 and decays when 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1. A factor in front, c axc\,a^xcax, sets the starting value.

y=3⋅2xy = 3\cdot 2^xy=3⋅2x starts at 3 and doubles every unit: 3, 6, 12, 24…

Logarithm

y=log⁡ax:  (1,0) ✓,x>0y = \log_a x:\ \ (1, 0)\ \checkmark, \quad x > 0y=loga​x:  (1,0) ✓,x>0

Inverse of axa^xax (mirror in y=xy = xy=x); asymptote x=0x = 0x=0.

The idea

log⁡ax\log_a xloga​x is the inverse of axa^xax: it passes through (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0), is defined only for x>0x > 0x>0, and has the yyy-axis as asymptote. It answers “to what power must I raise aaa to get xxx?”.

log⁡28=3\log_2 8 = 3log2​8=3 because 23=82^3 = 823=8 — the blue point. log⁡212=−1\log_2 \tfrac12 = -1log2​21​=−1 because 2−1=122^{-1} = \tfrac122−1=21​.

Rational (hyperbola)

y=ax+bcx+d:  x=−dc,  y=acy = \frac{ax + b}{cx + d}:\ \ x = -\frac dc,\ \ y = \frac acy=cx+dax+b​:  x=−cd​,  y=ca​

The two asymptotes; the centre of symmetry is where they meet.

The idea

y=ax+bcx+dy = \tfrac{ax + b}{cx + d}y=cx+dax+b​ is a hyperbola. The vertical asymptote is where the denominator vanishes, x=−dcx = -\tfrac dcx=−cd​; for large ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣ only the leading terms matter, so y→acy \to \tfrac acy→ca​, the horizontal asymptote.

Worked example

y=2x+1x−3y = \tfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}y=x−32x+1​: vertical asymptote x=3x = 3x=3, horizontal asymptote y=21=2y = \tfrac21 = 2y=12​=2.

y=xn,  y=x,  y=1x,  y=∣x∣y = x^n,\ \ y = \sqrt x,\ \ y = \frac1x,\ \ y = |x|y=xn,  y=x​,  y=x1​,  y=∣x∣

On (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1), x3<x2<x<xx^3 < x^2 < x < \sqrt xx3<x2<x<x​; beyond 1 the order reverses. The curves all cross at (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1).

Piecewise functions

f(x)={g(x)x<ah(x)x≥af(x) = \begin{cases} g(x) & x < a\\ h(x) & x \ge a\end{cases}f(x)={g(x)h(x)​x<ax≥a​

f(x)=x+1f(x) = x + 1f(x)=x+1 for x<1x < 1x<1 and 3−x3 - x3−x for x≥1x \ge 1x≥1: both give 2 at x=1x = 1x=1, so the two lines meet in a peak at (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2).

Zeros and intersections

Zeros

f(x)=0  ⟺  (x,0)f(x) = 0\iff (x, 0)f(x)=0⟺(x,0)

The idea

A zero is an xxx with f(x)=0f(x) = 0f(x)=0: where the graph meets the xxx-axis. To find them, factor if you can — a product is zero when one factor is.

Worked example

x2−x−6=(x−3)(x+2)=0x^2 - x - 6 = (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0x2−x−6=(x−3)(x+2)=0, so x=3x = 3x=3 or x=−2x = -2x=−2.

Bolzano

f(a) f(b)<0 ⇒ ∃ c∈(a,b): f(c)=0f(a)\,f(b) < 0 \ \Rightarrow\ \exists\,c \in (a, b):\ f(c) = 0f(a)f(b)<0 ⇒ ∃c∈(a,b): f(c)=0

For f continuous on [a, b]; with f monotonic the zero is unique.

The idea

A continuous function that is negative at one end of [a,b][a, b][a,b] and positive at the other must cross zero in between. Halving the interval and keeping the half with a sign change (bisection) traps the zero as tightly as you like.

Worked example

f(x)=x3+x−1f(x) = x^3 + x - 1f(x)=x3+x−1: f(0)=−1<0f(0) = -1 < 0f(0)=−1<0 and f(1)=1>0f(1) = 1 > 0f(1)=1>0, so there is a zero in (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1). f(0.5)=−0.375<0f(0.5) = -0.375 < 0f(0.5)=−0.375<0 moves it into (0.5,1)(0.5, 1)(0.5,1).

Number of solutions

f(x)=g(x)  ⟺  y=f ∩ y=gf(x) = g(x)\iff y = f \,\cap\, y = gf(x)=g(x)⟺y=f∩y=g

Count where the two graphs cross; for f(x) = k move the horizontal line y = k.

The idea

An equation f(x)=g(x)f(x) = g(x)f(x)=g(x) you cannot solve by algebra can still be understood: draw both graphs and count where they meet. Each intersection point is one solution; its xxx-coordinate is the value.

Worked example

ex=x+2e^x = x + 2ex=x+2: the exponential crosses the line twice — once near x≈−1.84x \approx -1.84x≈−1.84 and once near x≈1.15x \approx 1.15x≈1.15 — so there are 2 solutions.
